blocks.text: A probability is a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely an event is: 0 means it never happens, 1 means it always happens. Many situations unfold in stages. A parcel, for example, is first handed to a carrier and then arrives late or on time. A probability tree draws such a situation from left to right, with one set of branches for each stage and a probability written on every branch. A path is one route through the tree from the start to an end, taking one branch at each stage. Exactly one of the branches that leave a point is taken, so their probabilities add up to 1. The probabilities at a later stage may depend on what happened before: if a first choice changes what is left, the branches after it change too.

The branches of the second stage carry conditional probabilities. A conditional probability is the probability of one event given that another event is known to happen or to have happened. The probability of B given A is written P(B | A). In Figure 1, the 0.1 on the "Late" branch after "Van" is P(late | van): of the parcels that go by van, one in ten arrives late.

blocks.alt: A tree with two stages. First stage: van 0.7, bike 0.3. After van: late 0.1, on time 0.9. After bike: late 0.6, on time 0.4.
blocks.caption: Figure 1. A probability tree for the parcels of one depot. Each parcel is carried by van or by bike, and then arrives late or on time.

blocks.text: Two rules turn the tree into answers. First, multiply along a path: the probability that A and B both happen is
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A)
Second, add across paths: when an event can be reached by more than one path, its probability is the sum of the probabilities of those paths.

A tree also lets you turn a condition around. In general, P(A | B) is not the same as P(B | A). To find P(A | B), divide the probability of the path on which both A and B happen by the total probability of B, which the second rule gives:
P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B)

Two events are called independent if knowing that one has happened does not change the probability of the other, so that P(B | A) = P(B). If the probability of B depends on whether A has happened, the events are dependent.

P(late) = P(van) × P(late | van) + P(bike) × P(late | bike) is a weighted average of the two "late" branches, so it equals P(late | bike) only when both branches carry the same probability.

blocks.text: Computers spend much of their time looking things up: a name in a customer file, a word in a dictionary, a product in a catalogue. How long a search takes depends on the method and on the length of the list. To compare methods, we count checks. One check compares the wanted item with one item of the list.

Linear search is the simplest method. It checks the items one after another from the start of the list until it finds the wanted item or reaches the end. It works on any list, in any order. On a list of n items it needs one check if the wanted item comes first, and n checks if the item comes last or is not in the list at all.

Binary search is usually much faster on long lists, but it only works on a sorted list, here one that runs from the smallest item to the largest, in which the computer can go straight to any position. It checks the item in the middle. If that is the wanted item, the search is over. If the wanted item is smaller, it can only lie in the lower half, so the upper half is dropped together with the item just checked; if it is larger, the lower half and the checked item are dropped. The search then repeats on the part that is left, until the item is found or nothing is left. Where a part has two middle items, the lower one is checked. After each unsuccessful check, at most half of the items are still left.

blocks.caption: Table 1. The largest number of checks each method can need.
head: Items in the list
Linear search

blocks.text: Table 1 shows what this means for long lists. Compare the rows for 500 and 1,000 items: when a list becomes twice as long, the largest number of checks doubles for linear search, but grows by only one for binary search.

This speed has a price. A list must be sorted before binary search can be used, and sorting takes work. A sorted list must also be kept in order whenever items are added. For a short list, or for an unsorted list that is searched only once, linear search can therefore be the better choice.

questions.explanation: The last paragraph names the cases: a short list, or an unsorted list searched only once. The pile of exam papers is short, unsorted and searched once. The invoice archive is searched once but is already sorted; the article list is unsorted but searched thousands of times.

options.text: A phone keeps 2,000 contacts in alphabetical order, and the owner looks up names many times a day.
options.why: The list is already sorted and searched often, which is where binary search pays off.

options.text: A clerk looks once for one invoice, by its number, in an archive of 50,000 invoices sorted by number.
options.why: The archive is searched only once, but it is already sorted, so binary search can be used straight away and needs far fewer checks.

options.text: A teacher looks once for one paper in an unsorted pile of 30 exam papers.
options.why: The list is short and searched only once, so sorting it first would cost more than it saves.

options.text: A shop receives an unsorted list of a million article numbers and will look articles up in it thousands of times a day.
options.why: The list is unsorted, but it is long and searched very often, so sorting it once pays off many times over.

questions.stem: In which of these situations is linear search the more sensible method?

questions.explanation: Each linear search can need 1,000 checks, each binary search 10 (Table 1). After k searches the totals are 1,000 × k and 10,000 + 10 × k. For k = 10: 10,000 against 10,100, so sorting has not yet paid off. For k = 11: 11,000 against 10,110.

options.why: One linear search costs at most 1,000 checks. Sorting alone costs 10,000.
After 10 searches linear search has cost 10,000 checks. Sorting plus 10 binary searches costs 10,100, which is still more.
After 11 searches linear search has cost 11,000 checks, and sorting plus 11 binary searches 10,110.
Each binary search saves 990 checks over a linear one, so the cost of sorting is recovered after enough searches.

questions.stem: An unsorted list of 1,000 items will be searched several times. Sorting it once costs as much work as 10,000 checks. Counting the largest number of checks each search can need, from which search onwards is sorting first and then using binary search less work in total than using linear search every time?

blocks.text: The nucleus of a radioactive atom is unstable. Sooner or later it decays: it gives off radiation and usually becomes a different nucleus. When one particular nucleus will decay cannot be predicted; it happens at random. A sample of material, however, holds an enormous number of nuclei, and so many random events together follow a regular pattern.

The half-life of a radioactive isotope, written T½, is the time in which half of the radioactive nuclei present in a sample decay. For a single nucleus it is the time in which it has a 50% chance of decaying; across the many nuclei of a sample, that chance shows up as half of them decaying. During the next half-life, half of those that are left decay, and so on. After one half-life half of the nuclei remain, after two a quarter, after three an eighth. The number of radioactive nuclei left after a time t is

where N₀ is the number at the start. The quotient t ÷ T½ counts how many half-lives have passed; it need not be a whole number. Half-lives differ widely from one isotope to another, but the half-life of a given isotope is fixed: it does not depend on how large the sample is.

Nuclei cannot easily be counted, but their decays can. The activity A of a sample is the number of nuclei that decay per second. Its unit is the becquerel (Bq): 1 Bq is one decay per second. The activity is proportional to the number of radioactive nuclei present, so it halves in every half-life too:

Figure 1 shows how the activity of one sample falls over twelve hours. The curve falls steeply at first and then more and more slowly, because each half-life removes the same fraction of what is left, not the same amount. The half-life can be read from such a curve: it is the time the activity takes to fall from any value to half that value.

blocks.alt: A falling curve. Activity in becquerel against time in hours. It starts at 1,600 Bq at 0 hours and passes through 800 Bq at 3 hours, 400 Bq at 6 hours, 200 Bq at 9 hours, 100 Bq at 12 hours. The grid has a line every hour and every 200 Bq.
blocks.caption: Figure 1. The activity of a sample of one radioactive isotope over twelve hours.

blocks.text: An electric circuit is a closed path along which charge can flow. Three quantities describe it. The current I, measured in amperes (A), is how much charge passes a point each second. The voltage V, measured in volts (V), drives the current; a battery supplies it. The resistance R, measured in ohms (Ω), is how strongly a component opposes the current. For the resistors in this passage the three are linked by Ohm's law:
V = I × R

Resistors can be joined in two basic ways. In series they lie one after another on a single path, so the same current flows through each. For two resistors Ra and Rb their resistances add up, R = Ra + Rb, and the voltages across them add up to the voltage of the source. The larger resistance takes the larger share of the voltage.

In parallel the resistors sit on separate branches between the same two junctions, the points where the wire divides and joins again. Each branch therefore has the same voltage across it. The current divides at the first junction and comes together at the second; the currents in the branches add up to the current that arrives. The branch with the smaller resistance carries the larger current. The combined resistance R of two resistors Ra and Rb in parallel follows from

Adding a branch gives the current an extra path, so the combined resistance is always smaller than the smallest resistance in the group. A circuit that mixes both arrangements is solved in steps: replace each parallel group by its combined resistance, add the resistances in series, and use Ohm's law for the current.
A resistor turns electrical energy into heat. The power P, in watts (W), is the energy it converts each second:
P = V × I
Here V is the voltage across that resistor and I the current through it. Figure 1 shows a circuit with one resistor in series and two in parallel; the connecting wires have no resistance.

blocks.text: Before a firm launches a product, it wants to know how many units it must sell to avoid a loss. Break-even analysis answers this by sorting the costs into two kinds.

Fixed costs stay the same in total however many units are made, at least within the range of output the firm plans for. Rent and insurance are examples. Variable costs rise in proportion to output: for example, each unit needs the same amount of material, so the variable cost per unit stays the same. With F for the fixed costs, v for the variable cost per unit and q for the number of units, the total cost is
total cost = F + v × q

If each unit sells at the price p, revenue is p × q. The difference p − v is called the contribution margin per unit. Each unit sold contributes this amount, first towards covering the fixed costs and, once they are covered, towards profit:
profit = (p − v) × q − F
The break-even point is the number of units at which revenue equals total cost, so that profit is zero. Setting the profit to zero gives
break-even quantity = F ÷ (p − v)

Below this quantity the firm makes a loss; every unit beyond it adds the contribution margin to profit. The same reasoning tells the firm how many units it needs for a profit it aims at: the contribution margins must then cover the fixed costs and that profit together.

Figure 1 shows the monthly figures for one product. The revenue line starts at zero. The total cost line starts at the fixed costs, because they arise even if nothing is sold, and climbs more gently than the revenue line. The break-even point is where the two lines cross; to its right the gap between them is the profit. The analysis assumes that every unit made is sold and that the price and the variable cost per unit do not change with the number sold.

blocks.alt: Three straight lines, euros per month against units sold per month from 0 to 1,000. Fixed costs: a horizontal line at €6,000. Total cost: from €6,000 at 0 units to €16,000 at 1,000 units. Revenue: from €0 at 0 units to €25,000 at 1,000 units. Revenue and total cost cross at 400 units and €10,000. The grid has a line every 100 units and every €2,500.

blocks.text: When the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it. How much less is measured by the price elasticity of demand: the percentage change in the quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in the price.
elasticity = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price

A percentage change depends on the value it is measured from. A rise from 20 to 25 is 25% of 20, but a fall from 25 to 20 is only 20% of 25. To get the same answer in both directions, this passage uses the midpoint method, which measures every change against the average of the old and the new value:
% change = (new − old) ÷ ((new + old) ÷ 2) × 100

Because price and quantity normally move in opposite directions, the elasticity of demand is normally negative. What matters for most purposes is its size, ignoring the sign. Demand is called elastic if that size is greater than 1: the quantity changes by a larger percentage than the price. It is inelastic if the size is less than 1, and unit elastic if it is exactly 1.

Elasticity tells a seller what a price change does to revenue, the price times the quantity sold. If demand is elastic, a price rise lowers revenue, because the lost sales outweigh the higher price. If demand is inelastic, a price rise raises revenue. If demand is unit elastic, revenue stays the same. With the midpoint method these rules hold exactly.

Several things make demand more elastic. An important one is the number of close substitutes: if buyers can easily switch to something similar, they react strongly to a price rise. Demand for necessities, which people keep buying even when the price rises, tends to be inelastic. Time matters too: buyers react more to a price change over months than over days, because they have longer to find alternatives.

blocks.text: Researchers who want to know what a large group thinks or does rarely ask everyone. The population is the whole group they want to learn about, for example all students at one university. A sample is the part of it they actually study. They usually draw it from a sampling frame, a list of the members of the population such as the register of enrolled students. A sample is useful only if it is representative: it should resemble the population in the ways that matter for the question.

Four methods choose the sample by chance. In a simple random sample every member of the frame has the same chance of being chosen, and so does every possible group of the chosen size. A systematic sample starts at a randomly chosen place in the list and then takes every k-th member after it. A stratified sample first divides the population into groups that share a feature, called strata, such as the year of study, and then draws a random sample from every stratum, usually in proportion to its size; so every stratum is sure to be represented. A cluster sample divides the population into groups, called clusters, such as the halls of residence; it chooses some of the clusters at random and then includes every member of the chosen clusters.

A convenience sample consists of whoever is easy to reach, such as the people who pass a stand in the main hall one morning. In a voluntary response sample the researcher invites everyone to take part, for example through a link on a website, and the sample consists of those who choose to. Neither method gives the members of the population a known chance of being chosen.

Bias is a systematic difference between what a method's samples show and the population, one that would not average out if the sampling were repeated many times in the same way. Sampling bias arises when some members of the population are less likely to be chosen than others, in a way the researcher does not know or allow for. One cause is a frame that leaves people out: a sample drawn from a list of landline numbers cannot include anyone without a landline. A well-chosen sample can still end up biased. Non-response bias arises when some of the people chosen do not take part and differ from those who do in ways that matter for the question. Self-selection, as in a voluntary response sample, has a similar effect from the start: people with strong views on the topic are more likely to join.

Even an unbiased sample differs from the population by chance; another random sample would give a slightly different result. This sampling error becomes smaller as the sample grows, even in a biased survey. Bias does not: a biased method gives a biased result however large the sample is, and a larger sample only makes the wrong answer look more precise.

blocks.text: In logic, an argument is a set of statements in which some, the premises, are offered as reasons for another, the conclusion. For example: "All metals conduct electricity. Copper is a metal. So copper conducts electricity." Logic asks whether the premises really support the conclusion.

A deductive argument is valid if its form makes it impossible for all its premises to be true while its conclusion is false: no argument of the same form has true premises and a false conclusion. Validity depends only on the form of the argument, that is, its structure rather than its subject matter. It does not depend on whether the premises are in fact true. "All fish can fly. A trout is a fish. So a trout can fly." is valid: if both premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true as well. It is still a poor argument, because its first premise is false. An argument is sound if it is valid and all its premises are true. The conclusion of a sound argument must therefore be true. The copper argument is sound; the trout argument is valid but not sound.

Some forms are known by name. They start from a premise of the form "If P, then Q", in which P is called the antecedent and Q the consequent. Two forms are valid: modus ponens ("If P, then Q. P. So Q.") and modus tollens ("If P, then Q. Not Q. So not P."). Two forms look similar but are invalid: affirming the consequent ("If P, then Q. Q. So P.") and denying the antecedent ("If P, then Q. Not P. So not Q."). Take "If a plant gets no water, it wilts. This plant has wilted. So it got no water." The plant may have wilted from heat or disease, so the premises can be true while the conclusion is false: the argument affirms the consequent and is invalid. An invalid argument can happen to have true premises and a true conclusion; it is invalid because its premises do not guarantee its conclusion.

A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning. Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are formal fallacies: the error lies in the form itself. Informal fallacies cannot be detected from the form alone; spotting them depends on the content and context, and three are especially common in debate. An ad hominem attacks the person who makes a claim, their character or motives, instead of the claim. A straw man misrepresents an opponent's position, usually as something more extreme or weaker than it is, and then refutes that version. A false dilemma presents two options as the only ones when there are others. Spotting a fallacy shows that an argument fails to support its conclusion; it does not show that the conclusion is false.

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph: an ad hominem attacks the person, their character or motives, instead of the claim. Only the first reply does that. The second is a straw man, the third a false dilemma, and the fourth addresses the proposal itself.

options.text: "Sam only wants this because Sam never plans ahead, so we can ignore the argument."
options.why: This attacks Sam's character and motives instead of the proposal.

options.text: "Sam wants the library open all night, every night of the year, and we could never pay for that."
options.why: This replaces Sam's proposal with a more extreme one and attacks that: a straw man.

options.text: "Either we keep the present hours or we double the student fees, and nobody wants higher fees."
options.why: This offers two options as if they were the only ones: a false dilemma.

options.text: "Staying open until midnight would need two more staff each night, and the budget does not cover them."
options.why: This answers the proposal itself with a reason about cost. It may be right or wrong, but it is not a fallacy of the kinds in the text.

blocks.text: Some traits of plants and animals are passed on according to simple rules first described by Gregor Mendel, who crossed garden peas. A trait such as flower colour is controlled by a gene, which comes in different versions called alleles. A pea plant carries two alleles of each gene, one inherited from each parent. If the two are the same, the plant is homozygous for that gene; if they differ, it is heterozygous. The pair of alleles a plant carries is its genotype; the trait we can see is its phenotype.

In pea flowers the allele for violet, written V, is dominant over the allele for white, written v, which is recessive. A plant with at least one V has violet flowers, so VV and Vv plants look alike. Only a vv plant has white flowers. Not every gene behaves this way, but flower colour in peas does.

When a plant forms its gametes, the pollen and egg cells, its two alleles separate, and each gamete receives one of them, each with the same probability; this is called the law of segregation. Which allele an offspring receives from one parent is independent of which it receives from the other. The possible offspring of a cross can therefore be listed in a Punnett square, a grid with the alleles of one parent along the top and those of the other down the side; each of the four boxes is equally likely. For two Vv parents the boxes are VV, Vv, Vv and vv (the heterozygote fills two boxes): on average a quarter of the offspring are VV, a half Vv and a quarter vv, so three quarters have violet flowers and one quarter white.

A plant with violet flowers may be VV or Vv. To find out which, it can be crossed with a white plant, which can only pass on v; this is called a test cross. If the violet plant is Vv, about half of the offspring will be white; if it is VV, none will. Real counts only come close to the expected shares, because each offspring receives its alleles by chance. Table 1 shows the results of three crosses made by a gardener.
